background.definition: Urinary incontinence (UI) is any unintentional leakage of urine. European guidelines classify it as stress urinary incontinence (SUI), urge urinary incontinence (UUI) or mixed urinary incontinence. According to the International Continence Society, overactive bladder syndrome (OAB) is defined as "urinary urgency, usually accompanied by frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency urinary incontenence, in the absence of urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology".

Prevalence is higher in nursing home residents (45%-72%).

Costs have nearly doubled in the past 10 years.
Interference of activities due to embarrassment is an issue.

list.listitem: It is important to characterize the type and determine the underlying cause of incontinence.

A history of incontinence associated with coughing, sneezing, laughing, or other sources of bladder pressure suggests stress incontinence. Urine loss concomitant or immediately following an episode of urgency suggests urge incontinence.

Characterize type, frequency and timing of incontinence, any predisposing or exacerbating triggers such as sneezing or coughing (stress incontinence), presence of nocturia, whether sudden urgency (urge incontinence), or whether no inciting factors can be identified (overflow incontinence).
Take a medication history to determine drug causes ().
Past medical and surgical history to evaluate for benign prostatic hypertrophy, prostate cancer, or surgical treatment for either problem.
The Urinary Symptom Profile is a 13-item patient questionnaire that can be used to characterize incontinence based on symptoms.
European guidelines (2022) recommend a digital rectal exam to evaluate for enlarged or tender prostate, and an abdominal exam to detect an extended bladder.
Order a urinalysis to rule out infection and a post-void residual volume in newly diagnosed patients to rule out obstruction. A normal residual volume is less than 100 ml.
Ultrasound measurement of postvoid residual volume is a more comfortable alternative to catheterization.

Use of urodynamic testing and measures of urethral function such as urethral pressure pofilometry, Valsalva leak point pressure and retrograde urethral resistance may be considered on an individual basis but are not routinely recommended by 2022 European guidelines.

Treat underlying urinary retention if detected based on post-void residual.
Urge incontinence: Treatment options include oxybutynin, propiverine, tolterodine, or trospium, with the dose titrated to avoid adverse effects.

However a recent meta-analysis of 72 RCTs concluded that only ~20% of patients benefit from any pharmacotherapy (~10% achieve continence with little difference between different treatments, with the remaining having a decrease in incontinence episodes). About 3% patients discontinue treatment due to adverse effects.

Overactive bladder (OAB): Anticholinergic drugs (oxybutynin, tolterodine) during initial treatment reduce urination frequency and urine leadage episodes but can cause side effects such as dry mouth. Trospium 20 mg once or twice daily is effective for OAB. In a RCT, the combination of tolterodine and tamsulosin was more effective than either treatment alone in the management of men with lower urinary tract symptoms and overactive bladder.

Mirabegron (a beta3-adrenoceptor agonist) for use in the treatment of OAB was associated with one fewer episode of urinary incontinence every 2 to 3 days compared to placebo, but no differences in the frequency of nocturia. Mirabegron is associated with a relatively lower adverse effect profile compared to other anti-muscarinics.
A systematic review found that duloxetine in patients with stress incontinence post -prostatectomy was effective and is recommended by European 2022 guidelines.

Fesoterodine (an antimuscarinic agent used in the treatment of overactive bladder) use among 963 patients (average age 58 years) was associated with fewer urgency episodes (−1.28 vs. −1.07) and nocturia (−1.02 vs. −0.85) per 24 hours compared to placebo.
Vibegron (75 mg once daily) is associated with 1 fewer urge incontinence episode every 2 days compared to placebo, but not more effective than tolterodine.I

In men with overactive bladder symptoms receiving pharmacologic treatment for BPH, vibegron significantly reduced daily micturitions, urgency, nocturia, and incontinence episodes over 12 weeks compared to placebo, with a similar adverse event profile.
In higher-functioning nursing home residents, dual use of cholinesterase inhibitors (CI) and bladder anticholinergics may result in greater rates of functional decline than use of CIs alone.

Intravesical injection of 500 U of botulinum toxin A in patients with neurogenic detrusor instability can reduce the need of oral medication, reduce high detrusor pressure, reduce frequency of urinary leakage, and improve overall quality of life.

Implantation of an artificial urinary sphincter is an option and is recommended by AUA guidelines (2024), especially for men with more severe incontinence. A systematic review found generally favorable data from mostly observational studies that it reduced daily pads by 4, improved quality of life, and increased the dry rate to about 50% and the social dry rate to 80%.
The total reconstruction of the vesicourethral junction provides better outcomes than no reconstruction or anterior reconstruction in patients with post-prostatectomy incontinence.

Bone-anchored male sling is a minimally invasive treatment for postoperative male urinary incontinence, but is associated with significant morbidity and is not recommended by AUA guidelines (2024) for severe stress incontinence in men with post-prostatectomy incontinence. It can be considered in men who have not had radiation therapy, and who have minimal nocturnal incontinence or bothersome isolated climacturia.
Acupuncture is not helpful for BPH symptoms.
Biofeedback is effective in women for urge and mixed incontinence but has not been studied in men.

Among 855 women, a 12-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) exercise program for pregnant women at 20 to 36 weeks gestational age reduces urinary incontinence (42% vs. 53% control patients) in women in the third trimester of pregnancy.

A Cochrane review of 20 studies studying 21 comparisons and involving 1338 people demonstrated that behavioral interventions may reduce the mean number of incontinent episodes in 24 hours with little or no difference on patients quality of life. Other interventions such as interventions by continence nurse practitioners did not affect the frequency of people continent three months after treatment. Complementary therapies such as acupuncture, and physical therapies, such as transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation have some beneficial effect on frequency of continence and functional ability.

For postprostatectomy incontinence, the benefits of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) benefits are unclear but given the low cost and possible benefit may be considered. They are recommended by Europea guidelines based on a systematic review showing benefit.
Studies of transcutaneous electrical stimulation show mixed benefit based on a Cochrane review.
The main medical treatment for male urinary incontinence is to treat any underlying condition(s) that are causing the incontinence (e.g., prostatitis, UTI, or BPH.
Incontinence pads and indwelling catheters may be helpful.
Compression devices (penile clamps) may be used to manage long term incontinence but there are safety problems.

Lifestyle measures such as addressing obesity, exercise, diet, and fluid restrictions are often recommended. However, the benefit of lifestyle changes and extra-corporeal magnetic innervation have not been well studied. Similarly, the effectiveness of a combination of methods is inconclusive.
Timed voiding is sometimes recommended, but studies of timed voiding are few and of poor quality.
After adjusting for other factors likely to affect continence, 15.3% of men treated for prostate cancer with surgery were incontinent compared with 4.1% of patients treated with radiation. B

A clinical trial randomized men aged 50 to 69 years with localized, screen-detected prostate cancer (stage 1c or 2) to receive 1 of 3 management strategies: (1) active surveillance (AS) with frequent prostate-specific antigen tests and biopsy and/or treatment of significant elevations, (2) radiotherapy, or (3) radical prostatectomy. In general, urinary outcomes were worst for surgery and similar for AS or radiotherapy with regards to urinary function and worse for surgical therapy and radiation therapy for sexual function compared to AS.

Symptoms tend to improve gradually post-operatively. For example, for men with localized prostate cancer, most functional outcome differences related to treatment options are attenuated by 5 years. However, prostatectomy is associated with worse urinary incontinence and sexual function through 5 years than men who chose other treatment options. B
Incontinence is more common is strongly associated with increasing age. B
